result:
I find myself drawn, when given no constraints at all, to thinking about thresholds—the strange in-between spaces where one thing becomes another. Not metaphorically at first, just literally: a doorway. The moment your foot is neither fully in one room nor the other. There's a word for this in anthropology, *liminality*, coined to describe the middle stage of rites of passage, when a person is no longer a child but not yet an adult, no longer single but not yet married, stripped of their old status and not yet given the new one. Van Gennep noticed this a century ago, and Victor Turner ran with it, and now the word has escaped academia entirely and gotten loose in internet culture, attached to photographs of empty parking garages and fluorescent-lit hallways at 3 a.m. People feel something looking at those images, a kind of pleasant dread, and I think what they're responding to is the absence of narrative pressure. A liminal space is a place where nothing is supposed to be happening. You're not meant to linger in a hallway. You're meant to pass through it. So when you see one empty and still, photographed with nobody walking through it, it feels like catching architecture in its underwear, doing nothing, waiting.

I keep thinking about waiting as its own category of experience, distinct from boredom, though they share a border. Boredom is when time has no content. Waiting is when time has exactly one piece of content, suspended just out of reach, and everything else is just static around it. A waiting room is named with perfect honesty—it is a room for waiting, nothing else happens there, even though everything that happens there is incidental: the magazines, the muted television, the other people's coughs. The room itself has been built around an absence, the way a keyhole is built around the shape of a key that isn't there.

I don't know why this interests me more than, say, writing about a concrete subject with a beginning and an end. Maybe because thresholds are honest about something that finished narratives tend to hide: that most of experience doesn't resolve. Stories have a bias toward resolution because resolution is satisfying and our brains reward pattern completion with something like pleasure. But actual days are mostly threshold. You wake up not fully awake. You eat breakfast while still thinking about a dream. You arrive at work five minutes early and sit in the car. None of this is the "content" of your life, by the usual accounting, and yet it might be most of your life, measured in minutes.

There's a similar feeling in language, in the gap between two words, or in the pause before you remember the word you're looking for. Linguists have a term for that too—*tip-of-the-tongue* phenomenon—where you can feel the shape of a word, its syllable count, sometimes even its first letter, without being able to produce it. The word is present and absent simultaneously, which is its own kind of threshold. I wonder if thought in general works this way more than we admit: less like a line of finished sentences and more like a series of doorways you're constantly half-through, catching yourself mid-revision, mid-correction, mid-doubt.

Maybe this is why dusk and dawn get so much more poetic attention than noon or midnight. Noon and midnight are absolutes—you know exactly where you are in the day. Dusk and dawn are negotiations. The light hasn't decided what it's going to be yet. Painters have always known this; the "golden hour" obsession in photography is really just liminality with better marketing. But it's not only about beauty. There's something almost ethical in the in-between, a kind of humility. Noon insists. Dusk suggests.

I could go further and say that whole identities live in this threshold state. Adolescence is the most obvious one, the literal subject of Van Gennep's original observation, but there are others less discussed: the early months of a new job, when you don't yet know the unwritten rules but have stopped being able to claim total ignorance as an excuse. The year after a divorce, when your legal status has changed but your habits haven't caught up; you still reach for two coffee cups some mornings. Grief generally seems to be a long threshold, maybe the longest one most people pass through, where the world insists the person is gone and your nervous system continues, for a while, to act as if they might still walk through the door.

What strikes me about all these examples is that the threshold is usually treated as a problem to be solved quickly, a discomfort to be minimized. Get through training as fast as possible. Get over the breakup. Don't dwell. But I wonder if something gets lost in the rush to resolve, some kind of information that's only available while you're unresolved. Turner thought liminal periods were socially valuable precisely because the normal rules were suspended—initiates in a rite of passage are allowed, even expected, to behave in ways forbidden before and after, because the old self has been dismantled and the new self hasn't been built yet, and in that brief architectural gap, you can see the studs and wiring of the self that's usually hidden behind drywall.

I don't have a tidy place to land this, which feels appropriate, given the subject. Maybe the right ending for a piece about thresholds is just another threshold: not a conclusion, but a doorway left open, the kind you're not sure yet whether you're walking into or out of.
